concept.name: Stationarity
concept.definition: The property of a stochastic process whose statistical behavior does not change over time. A strictly stationary process has all joint distributions invariant to time shifts; in practice stationarity usually means a flat-looking series with no trend, constant variance, a constant autocorrelation structure, and no periodic fluctuations.
concept.intuition: A stationary series behaves the same in 2020 as in 2010: it fluctuates around a stable level with stable variability, so its past behavior is a usable guide to its future behavior.
concept.mechanics: Stationarity is assessed from run-sequence plots, ACF behavior, and formal unit-root tests (e.g., augmented Dickey-Fuller). Non-stationary series are transformed by differencing (Y_t = Z_t - Z_{t-1}), detrending (modeling residuals from a fitted trend), or variance-stabilizing transforms such as the logarithm.
concept.formula: Strict stationarity: for all h and k, the joint distribution of (X_t1, ..., X_tk) equals that of (X_{t1+h}, ..., X_{tk+h}). Differencing operator: Y_t = Z_t - Z_{t-1}.
concept.failure_modes: Applying stationary methods (ARMA, ordinary regression) to non-stationary data yields spurious regressions with misleadingly high R-squared and significance. Structural breaks can make a locally stationary model fail even when tests pass.
concept.misconceptions: That a stationary series must have no variation (it only needs time-invariant statistical properties), and that detrending and differencing are interchangeable (they address different types of non-stationarity).
concept.example: Daily S&P 500 returns are approximately stationary, fluctuating around a near-constant mean; the price level is non-stationary and is typically differenced (into returns) before fitting an ARMA model.

citations.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, Section 6.4.4.2 Stationarity
